metadata.summary: This international expert consensus addresses the diagnosis and management of Chiari malformation type 1 in children, including associated syringomyelia and related craniovertebral conditions. Its statements cover surgical indications, choice of procedure, assessment of outcomes, re-intervention and follow-up, as well as the evaluation and treatment of isolated pediatric syringomyelia. Consensus was reached on 58 statements; a proposed definition of radiological surgical failure did not reach consensus.

target_population: Infants and toddlers with CM1 and associated malformations
therapeutic_areas: Bony decompression of the posterior fossa

recognition: A painful, closed subcutaneous CSF collection

management.severity: Symptomatic leakage or symptomatic CSF collection
management.actions: Surgically revise the duraplasty and operative cavity; add external lumbar drainage if needed.

prevention: Use a watertight dural closure with non-resorbable stitches and securely close the muscle and soft tissues.
Preserve the arachnoid membrane when arachnoiditis is absent.

toxicities.event: Postoperative subcutaneous CSF collection without symptoms
recognition: A closed subcutaneous CSF collection without symptoms or cosmetic impact

management.actions: Use conservative management initially, which may include diuretic therapy, steroids, a bandage, or observation.

management.severity: Collection that persists or enlarges despite conservative management
management.actions: Reassess the diagnosis and consider whether another operation is needed.

recognition: Clinical or radiological recurrence after surgery

management.severity: Postoperative arachnoiditis associated with surgical failure
management.actions: Consider revision surgery to release adhesions and/or coagulate or resect the tonsils. In selected cases with multiple recurrences, IV ventricle stenting may be considered to maintain obex patency; its role remains debated.

prevention: Avoid entering the subarachnoid space during duraplasty unless arachnoiditis is present.
Limit subpial tonsillar coagulation because it adds morbidity and a risk of arachnoid scarring.
Prevent CSF leakage, which can predispose to arachnoiditis.
Avoid an excessively wide opening of the occipital squama.
When hydrocephalus accompanies CM1, treat the hydrocephalus before posterior fossa decompression to limit postoperative complications.

associated_therapies: Bony decompression of the posterior fossa
prevention: Avoid C2 laminectomy and extensive muscle stripping where possible.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Close the dura watertight, preferably with non-resorbable stitches, and securely close the muscle and soft tissues to help prevent CSF leakage.
Keep the arachnoid intact when arachnoiditis is absent to reduce CSF leakage and later scarring.
prophylaxis.target_population: Children with CM1 undergoing decompression with duraplasty without arachnoiditis

prophylaxis.recommendation: Avoid a broad occipital squama opening to reduce the risk of cerebellar ptosis.
prophylaxis.target_population: Children undergoing bony posterior fossa decompression

prophylaxis.recommendation: Avoid extensive muscle stripping and C2 laminectomy where possible to lower the risk of craniovertebral instability.
prophylaxis.target_population: Children undergoing bony posterior fossa decompression

prophylaxis.recommendation: Treat hydrocephalus before considering CM1 decompression to relieve raised intracranial pressure and limit postoperative complications.
prophylaxis.target_population: Symptomatic children with CM1 and hydrocephalus

infection_management.prevention: Prevent postoperative CSF leakage, which the document identifies as a predisposing factor for infection and subsequent arachnoiditis.

therapies_index.name: conservative management
approved_indications: Children with asymptomatic CM1 without syringomyelia, including those with marked tonsillar descent.
Children with asymptomatic, isolated and stable syringomyelia.
Children with an asymptomatic postoperative CSF collection, as the initial approach.
monitoring: For incidentally identified, asymptomatic CM1 without syringomyelia, continue neurological assessment and whole neuraxis MRI until growth ends, using an individualized schedule.
For isolated syringomyelia, tailor clinical and imaging follow-up to the child.
Reassess a postoperative CSF collection if it persists or enlarges.

therapies_index.name: diuretic therapy
approved_indications: An option within conservative care for an asymptomatic, closed postoperative CSF collection.
monitoring: Reassess the collection if it persists or increases.

therapies_index.name: steroids
approved_indications: An option within conservative care for an asymptomatic, closed postoperative CSF collection.
monitoring: Reassess the collection if it persists or increases.

therapies_index.name: bandage
approved_indications: An option within conservative care for an asymptomatic, closed postoperative CSF collection.
monitoring: Reassess the collection if it persists or increases.

therapies_index.name: treatment of hydrocephalus
therapies_index.mechanism: Restores CSF pathways and reduces raised intracranial pressure.
approved_indications: Treat hydrocephalus before considering CM1 surgery in a symptomatic child with both conditions; address CM1 subsequently if symptoms remain.
monitoring: Assess whether CM1-related symptoms persist after intracranial pressure is adequately controlled.

therapies_index.name: endoscopic third ventriculostomy
approved_indications: Described as a treatment for hydrocephalus associated with CM1 and syringomyelia; improvement after the procedure can make separate CM1 or syrinx treatment unnecessary.

therapies_index.name: cranial vault surgery
approved_indications: Treatment of craniosynostosis associated with CM1; it may also address cerebellar tonsillar ectopia.
monitoring: Evaluate persistent CM1 and its symptoms after treatment of craniosynostosis.

therapies_index.name: vault remodeling
approved_indications: The initial surgical approach for infants with syndromic craniosynostosis and CM1, with remodeling selected for the syndrome.

therapies_index.name: cranioplasty
approved_indications: Described as a previous operation in children with syndromic craniosynostosis and persistent CM1; subsequent surgery depends in part on its results.
monitoring: Consider the cranial volume achieved and persistent CM1 when evaluating further surgery.

therapies_index.name: posterior vault osteogenic distraction
approved_indications: May be considered before posterior fossa decompression in toddlers with CM1, polisynostosis and predominant brachycephaly, and in selected children of other ages.

therapies_index.name: posterior distraction
approved_indications: An option restricted to selected children with synostotic brachycephaly and associated CM1; it may address both conditions.

therapies_index.name: foramen magnum decompression
approved_indications: The principal surgical treatment for pediatric CM1 after predisposing factors, such as hydrocephalus, have been addressed.
monitoring: Assess clinical outcome and whole neuraxis MRI at 6 and 12 months; cine-MRI may assist.
After successful surgery, individualize clinical and whole neuraxis MRI follow-up for at least 10 years or until growth ends.

therapies_index.name: bony decompression of the posterior fossa alone
approved_indications: Could be performed for symptomatic CM1 without syringomyelia if the family accepts that another operation might be needed.
A small or asymptomatic syrinx may also be managed with bone-only decompression; the presence of syringomyelia does not make duraplasty an absolute requirement.
therapies_index.administration: Decompress the foramen magnum and include C1 laminectomy; avoid extending the opening to C2.
key_toxicities: Persistent or recurrent symptoms may necessitate another operation.
An opening that is too small or subsequent bone regrowth can cause failure.
Extensive dissection or C2 laminectomy can increase craniovertebral instability risk; an overly broad occipital opening can cause cerebellar ptosis.
CSF leakage can occur, although very rarely.
monitoring: Assess symptoms and whole neuraxis MRI at 6 and 12 months; cine-MRI may help.
In selected cases of suspected inadequate decompression, use 3D CT scan to assess the bone opening.
After successful surgery, individualize clinical and whole neuraxis MRI follow-up for at least 10 years or until growth ends.

therapies_index.name: bony decompression + duraplasty
approved_indications: Preferred for children with CM1 and syringomyelia, while recognizing that this is not an absolute rule for every syrinx.
key_toxicities: Duraplasty carries a higher complication risk than bone-only decompression, particularly CSF leakage-related complications.
monitoring: Assess clinical outcome and whole neuraxis MRI at 6 and 12 months; cine-MRI may help.
After successful surgery, individualize clinical and whole neuraxis MRI follow-up for at least 10 years or until growth ends.

therapies_index.name: duraplasty
approved_indications: Preferred in CM1 when syringomyelia and marked symptoms are present, subject to individualized surgical judgment.
May be used during revision surgery when further decompression is needed.
therapies_index.administration: Preserve the arachnoid when arachnoiditis is absent and make the dural closure capacious and watertight.
key_toxicities: Higher complication risk than bone-only decompression, particularly CSF leakage.
Incomplete expansion, arachnoid scarring and wound complications can adversely affect outcome.
monitoring: Assess clinical outcome and whole neuraxis MRI at 6 and 12 months; cine-MRI may help.
After successful surgery, individualize clinical and whole neuraxis MRI follow-up for at least 10 years or until growth ends.

therapies_index.name: C1 laminectomy
approved_indications: Included in the recommended extent of bony decompression for pediatric CM1.

therapies_index.name: cerebellar tonsils coagulation/resection
approved_indications: Indicated for very low-lying tonsils and recurrent or residual syringomyelia; the discussion also limits its consideration to selected cases of severe hindbrain dysfunction.
key_toxicities: Adds morbidity and a risk of arachnoid scarring.

therapies_index.name: autologous grafts
approved_indications: A preferred dural patch option for duraplasty, alongside allografts, according to surgeon preference.

therapies_index.name: allografts
approved_indications: A preferred dural patch option for duraplasty, alongside autologous grafts, according to surgeon preference.

therapies_index.name: watertight suture
approved_indications: Dural closure during pediatric CM1 surgery.
therapies_index.administration: Use non-resorbable stitches together with tight closure of muscle and soft tissue.

therapies_index.name: adhesiolysis
approved_indications: Treatment of posterior fossa arachnoiditis contributing to failure of CM1 surgery.
Treatment of symptomatic or progressive syringomyelia secondary to arachnoiditis after trauma or surgery; results in this setting may be disappointing.

therapies_index.name: IV ventricle stenting
approved_indications: A possible adjunct in selected cases of recurrent syringomyelia or repeated failure related to posterior fossa arachnoiditis; its role remains under debate.

therapies_index.name: surgical revision of the duraplasty and the surgical cavity
approved_indications: An open CSF leak or a symptomatic postoperative CSF collection.
therapies_index.administration: External lumbar drainage may be added if needed.

therapies_index.name: external lumbar drainage
approved_indications: An adjunct, if needed, to surgical revision for an open CSF leak or symptomatic postoperative CSF collection.

therapies_index.name: de-tethering procedure
approved_indications: Treatment of tethered cord syndrome in the rare child who also has CM1, to prevent neuro-urological deterioration; it does not affect CM1.
Etiological treatment of syringomyelia associated with spinal dysraphism.

therapies_index.name: intradural section of the filum terminale
approved_indications: Recommended solely to treat tethered cord syndrome in children with CM1; it has no role in treating the CM1 syndrome.

therapies_index.name: extradural section of the filum terminale
posterior reduction
approved_indications: An initial approach for symptomatic basilar invagination associated with CM1 without atlanto-axial instability; anterior decompression may follow if reduction fails.
monitoring: Determine whether the odontoid is reducible and whether compression and symptoms persist.

therapies_index.name: anterior decompression
approved_indications: Could be used for symptomatic basilar invagination associated with CM1 without atlanto-axial instability after posterior reduction fails.
May be indicated if symptomatic compression persists after reduction and posterior fixation for basilar invagination with atlanto-axial instability.
therapies_index.administration: In the described approach after failed posterior reduction, it is followed by posterior fusion.

therapies_index.name: posterior fusion
approved_indications: Described as following anterior decompression for symptomatic basilar invagination associated with CM1 when posterior reduction has failed.

therapies_index.name: posterior fixation
approved_indications: Preferred for basilar invagination with atlanto-axial dislocation, with reduction when symptomatic.

therapies_index.name: CVJ fixation
approved_indications: Used with posterior decompression for CM with documented CVJ instability and related symptoms; fixation is not indicated for CM1 without documented instability.
therapies_index.administration: Select instrumentation according to local anatomy, including the vertebral artery course and relevant bone dimensions.

therapies_index.name: C0–C3 fixation
approved_indications: An anatomical option for CM with CVJ instability; selection relative to C1–C2 fixation depends on local anatomy.

therapies_index.name: C1–C2 fixation
approved_indications: An anatomical option for CM with CVJ instability; selection relative to C0–C3 fixation depends on local anatomy.

therapies_index.name: posterior decompression and CVJ fixation
approved_indications: The preferred surgical option for a patient with CM, documented CVJ instability and related symptoms.

therapies_index.name: tumor removal
therapies_index.mechanism: Treats syringomyelia by removing its associated spinal cord tumor.
approved_indications: Syringomyelia associated with a spinal cord tumor.

therapies_index.name: spino-peritoneal, spino-subarachnoidal, or spino-pleural shunt
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides direct drainage of the syrinx.
approved_indications: May be performed for symptomatic or progressive syringomyelia after prior etiological treatments, including de-tethering, tumor removal or adhesiolysis, have failed; direct syrinx treatment is not advised routinely.

conditions.name: Chiari malformation type 1 (CM1)
conditions.description: In the absence of a better radiological definition, CM1 is identified when one or both cerebellar tonsils descend ≥ 5 mm below McRae’s line, or descend 3 to 5 mm with syringomyelia or a peg-like tonsillar appearance. The degree of descent alone has limited clinical correlation; tonsillar morphology and posterior fossa volume also matter. Transient descent caused by hydrocephalus or another mass effect is classified as acquired tonsillar ectopia rather than CM1.
conditions.epidemiology: The document describes CM1 as rare and notes that diagnoses have become increasingly frequent.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The main findings of Chiari syndrome include cough headache, brainstem, cerebellar or spinal cord dysfunction, otoneurological symptoms and scoliosis. Headache attributed to CM1 may be triggered by coughing or Valsalva, occur in the occipital or suboccipital region and last a few minutes. Many children diagnosed incidentally remain asymptomatic.

subtypes.name: asymptomatic children with incidentally discovered, isolated CM1 and no syringomyelia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: No reported CM1 symptoms or associated syringomyelia; tonsillar descent alone, including ≥ 20 mm, does not determine a surgical indication.

subtypes.name: CM1 children with syringomyelia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An associated spinal cord cavity affects surgical planning and the assessment of postoperative outcome.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess tonsillar position and morphology, the posterior fossa and associated findings.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation of suspected CM1.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Descent ≥ 5 mm below McRae’s line, or descent of 3 to 5 mm accompanied by syringomyelia or peg-like tonsils, meets the consensus radiological definition; descent alone has limited clinical correlation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify or exclude associated syringomyelia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In children with CM1.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Exclude acquired tonsillar ectopia associated with CSF hypotension.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When intracranial hypotension is a possible explanation for tonsillar descent.

diagnostic_workup.test: clinical assessment, fundoscopy and venous angio-MRI
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Exclude raised ICP as an explanation for acquired tonsillar ectopia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When intracranial hypertension is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further assess suspected raised ICP.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If needed after other assessments.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish headache attributable to CM1 from migraine or other causes, identify co-pathologies and evaluate children who may have difficulty communicating symptoms.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In children with CM1 and headache, brainstem, cerebellar or cervical cord symptoms or signs, or cognitive or behavioral disorders.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide supplementary information alongside clinical and other instrumental assessments.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In selected children when clinical or radiological findings warrant assessment; not as a routine first-line examination.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Their diagnostic and evaluative role in CM1 is unproven.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide supplementary information alongside clinical and other instrumental assessments.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In selected children when clinical or radiological findings warrant assessment; not as a routine first-line examination.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Their diagnostic and evaluative role in CM1 is unproven.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide supplementary information alongside clinical and other instrumental assessments.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In selected children when clinical or radiological findings warrant assessment; not as a routine first-line examination.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Their diagnostic and evaluative role in CM1 is unproven.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm suspected sleep apnea.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In very young children (< 6 years), when apnea is suspected or when cerebellar tonsillar descent is severe.

follow_up.schedule: For asymptomatic children with incidentally discovered CM1 and no syringomyelia, neurological and imaging follow-up continues until the end of growth; timing is individualized according to clinical findings and tonsillar herniation. Controls at 1, 3, and 5 years are mentioned as examples rather than a fixed schedule. Following successful surgery, individualized clinical and imaging follow-up continues for at least 10 years, or until the end of growth.
recommended_tests: Brain and whole spinal cord MRI when imaging follow-up is planned.
After surgery, clinical evaluation and whole neuraxis MRI at 6 and 12 months; cine-MRI may help but is not required in every case.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Although most asymptomatic children remain stable, clinical or radiological progression cannot be excluded in a minority. Persistent symptoms 12 months after surgery meet the accepted clinical definition of surgical failure. Persistent radiological findings must be interpreted in their clinical context; the proposed definition of radiological failure at 24 months did not achieve consensus.

conditions.name: CM 1.5
conditions.description: The document discusses CM 1.5 in relation to basilar invagination or impressio basilaris and possible craniovertebral junction instability; it does not provide a separate radiological definition.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms related to associated basilar invagination or impressio basilaris determine whether an operation is needed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate craniovertebral junction instability as a possible cause of persistent symptoms after surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly when instability is suspected in a patient with CM 1.5.

conditions.name: syringomyelia
conditions.description: Syringomyelia denotes a longitudinally oriented fluid-filled spinal cord cavity that extends upward and/or downward from its widest region. The classification used in the document distinguishes 4 types; type I-a is associated with CM1. Not every spinal cord fluid cavity qualifies as syringomyelia, and distinguishing it from central canal dilatation can be difficult.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Typical manifestations include dysesthesia, sensory disturbance or pain in corresponding dermatomes provoked by Valsalva, coughing, laughter or sneezing. Motor deficits tend to occur later. A centrally located syrinx typically produces dissociated sensory loss, whereas posterior horn involvement may cause burning neuropathic pain that is constant and worsens at rest.

subtypes.name: type I-a
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The type in the document’s 4-type classification that is associated with CM1.

subtypes.name: syringomyelia associated with CM1
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Its size, progression and symptoms influence decisions about CM1 surgery and postoperative assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a syrinx in children with CM1 and assess its extent.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In children with CM1.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The distinction between syringomyelia and central canal dilatation may be uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess postoperative persistence or change in associated syringomyelia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At 6 and 12 months after CM1 surgery and during individualized long-term follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The clinical significance of an unchanged syrinx must be considered alongside symptoms; a radiological definition of failure at 24 months did not reach consensus.

follow_up.schedule: After CM1 surgery, clinical evaluation and whole neuraxis MRI are used at 6 and 12 months. An asymptomatic syrinx still present at MRI at 12 months is followed closely; scoliosis or new symptoms prompt consideration of reoperation. After successful surgery, individualized follow-up continues for at least 10 years, or until the end of growth.
recommended_tests: Clinical assessment for symptoms and scoliosis.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The proposed syrinx-size threshold for surgery in an asymptomatic child, > 5 mm or > 8 mm, remains debated. Evidence relating cavity size to symptoms is limited, whereas progression is considered a clearer concern.

conditions.name: syringobulbia
conditions.description: This term refers to a longitudinally oriented fluid-filled cavity in the brain stem, extending upward and/or downward from its widest region.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms associated with syringobulbia in patients with CM-I usually follow a chronic course and include headache, gait or balance disturbance, limb weakness or dysesthesia, IX and X cranial nerve dysfunction, persistent hiccup, oscillopsia, nystagmus, Horner syndrome and central hypoventilation syndrome.

conditions.name: isolated/non-CM1 pediatric syringomyelia
conditions.description: A spinal cord syrinx occurring without CM1 may have different underlying causes. Because it is often clinically silent, identifying its cause relies heavily on imaging.
conditions.epidemiology: The document describes nonCM1 syringomyelia as likewise frequent, without providing a rate. Asymptomatic, isolated and stable syringomyelia has a low reported risk of evolution.
conditions.clinical_presentation: It is often asymptomatic. Neurological or neurophysiological deterioration, cavity enlargement and progressive scoliosis in association with a large syrinx are relevant signs of progression.

subtypes.name: syringomyelia-associated dysraphism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The associated spinal dysraphism directs treatment toward de-tethering.

subtypes.name: syringomyelia associated with spinal cord tumor
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An associated tumor directs treatment toward tumor removal.

subtypes.name: syringomyelia secondary to arachnoiditis due to previous trauma and/or surgery
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Symptomatic or progressive disease may require treatment of arachnoid adhesions; surgical results may be disappointing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify associated abnormalities, particularly spinal dysraphism.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation of non-Chiari syringomyelia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate an associated spinal cord tumor or vascular malformation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During etiological assessment of non-Chiari syringomyelia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate congenital or acquired CVJ or spinal instability.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When instability is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Look for an associated arachnoid cyst or signs of arachnoiditis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During selected etiological evaluations.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Arachnoiditis may be difficult to establish, and the technique is not completely sensitive.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Look for an associated arachnoid cyst or signs of arachnoiditis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In very selected cases.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Arachnoiditis may be difficult to establish, and the technique is not completely sensitive.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor for symptoms or enlargement of an asymptomatic isolated syrinx.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During individualized follow-up.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify deterioration relevant to a surgical decision.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When progression is being evaluated.

follow_up.schedule: Asymptomatic isolated syringomyelia is followed clinically and radiologically on a timetable tailored to the child; no fixed interval is specified.
recommended_tests: Clinical assessment for emerging symptoms and scoliosis.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: A stable, isolated syrinx in an asymptomatic child has a low reported risk of evolution. Progressive scoliosis is a possible marker of progression when associated with a large syrinx, rather than idiopathic hydromyelia.

conditions.name: Hydromyelia
conditions.description: Hydromyelia is described as a thin, centrally positioned dilatation within the spinal cord. The document distinguishes thin hydromyelia from a clinically significant syrinx and describes it as a para-physiological finding.
conditions.clinical_presentation: It is usually asymptomatic. The document notes that idiopathic hydromyelia commonly coexists with scoliosis, but does not treat that combination as the same surgical indication as progressive scoliosis with a large syrinx.

conditions.name: acquired tonsillar ectopia
conditions.description: This is tonsillar descent attributable to hydrocephalus, another source of mass effect, intracranial hypotension or intracranial hypertension, rather than CM1 when the descent is transient and related to the underlying condition.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate CSF hypotension as the cause of acquired tonsillar descent.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When distinguishing acquired ectopia from CM1.

diagnostic_workup.test: clinical assessment, fundoscopy and venous angio-MRI
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate raised ICP as the cause of acquired tonsillar descent.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When distinguishing acquired ectopia from CM1.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further investigate raised ICP.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If needed.

conditions.name: CM1 children with non-syndromic craniosynostosis
conditions.description: Non-syndromic craniosynostosis is discussed as a potential cause of acquired CM1. The document identifies oxycephaly, sagittal synostosis and posterior lambdoid synostosis among the relevant forms.

conditions.clinical_presentation: The discussion identifies neuro-urological deterioration as an outcome that de-tethering seeks to prevent; it does not give a fuller symptom profile.

special_populations.population: Asymptomatic children with incidentally discovered CM1 without syringomyelia
special_populations.considerations: Tonsillar descent alone, including ectopia ≥ 20 mm, does not establish a surgical indication. Clinical or radiological progression remains possible in a minority of children.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Surgery is not indicated. Neurological follow-up and whole neuraxis MRI should continue until the end of growth, with timing tailored to the clinical picture and degree of tonsillar herniation.

special_populations.population: Asymptomatic children with CM1 and syringomyelia
special_populations.considerations: Syrinx size and progression influence the decision to operate; the size threshold remains debated.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Surgery is indicated for a syrinx larger than 5–8 mm or a smaller syrinx that is enlarging.

special_populations.considerations: The document does not identify an etiological relationship between CM1 and epilepsy.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: CM1 surgery should not be offered to improve seizure control.

special_populations.population: Children with CM1 and cognitive and/or behavioral disorders
special_populations.considerations: Communication difficulties may obscure CM1 symptoms, and clinical signs may be difficult to recognize. Careful clinical and instrumental assessment, including neuro-pediatric evaluation, is mandatory.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: When clear CM1 symptoms are absent, surgery is not indicated to improve cognitive or behavioral problems.

special_populations.population: Very young children with CM1, suspected apneas, or severe cerebellar tonsillar descent
special_populations.considerations: Sleep-disordered breathing can occur in children with CM1.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Polysomnography is indicated in very young children (< 6 years), when apneas are suspected, and when tonsillar descent is severe.

special_populations.population: Symptomatic children with CM1 and hydrocephalus
special_populations.considerations: Raised intracranial pressure may account for symptoms and increase the risk of complications following posterior fossa decompression.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Treat hydrocephalus first; CM1 may be treated subsequently if symptoms persist.

special_populations.population: Children with CM1 and non-syndromic craniosynostosis
special_populations.considerations: Craniosynostosis may contribute to acquired tonsillar ectopia.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Treat the craniosynostosis before considering treatment of CM1; reassess CM1 if symptoms persist after the synostosis has resolved.

special_populations.population: Children with CM1 and syndromic craniosynostosis
special_populations.considerations: Management depends on the syndrome, cranial and posterior fossa volumes, previous operations, symptoms, and associated syringomyelia. Before craniovertebral decompression, Angio-RM or angio-CT is mandatory to exclude anomalous subcutaneous drainage.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: In infants, surgery should first expand cranial volume through syndrome-appropriate vault remodeling. For toddlers with polisynostosis and prevalent brachycephaly, posterior vault osteogenic distraction could be considered before posterior fossa decompression; it may also be considered in selected children of other ages.

special_populations.population: Children with CM1 and tethered cord syndrome
special_populations.considerations: This combination is rare. De-tethering addresses the tethered cord syndrome but has no effect on CM1; an association between CM1 and “occult tethered spinal cord” has never been demonstrated.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Perform de-tethering to prevent neuro-urological deterioration when tethered cord syndrome is present. Intradural section of the filum terminale is recommended only to treat tethered cord syndrome; extradural section is not recommended for either tethered cord syndrome or CM1.

special_populations.population: Children with CM1 and documented CVJ instability or symptomatic basilar invagination
special_populations.considerations: Surgical selection depends on symptoms, instability, and local anatomy. CVJ fixation is not indicated without documented instability.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For CVJ instability with related symptoms, posterior decompression and CVJ fixation are preferred. For symptomatic basilar invagination without atlanto-axial instability, anterior decompression could be considered if posterior reduction has failed; basilar invagination with atlanto-axial dislocation favors posterior fixation.

special_populations.population: Children with asymptomatic, isolated, stable syringomyelia
special_populations.considerations: The reported risk of progression is low. Follow-up should be individualized and include clinical and radiological assessment.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Surgery is not indicated while the syringomyelia remains asymptomatic and stable. If symptoms or progression develop, treatment should address its cause; direct shunting is considered only after etiological treatment fails.

special_populations.considerations: Persistent radiological tonsillar descent alone is not regarded as surgical failure. Persistent symptoms must be assessed alongside clinical and radiological findings.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Observe asymptomatic children with persistent tonsillar descent or syringomyelia; consider re-operation if symptoms or scoliosis develop. Children with persistent symptoms and unchanged MRI or syringomyelia at 6 or 12 months should be re-operated on. After successful surgery, continue clinical and whole neuraxis MRI follow-up for at least 10 years or until the end of growth.

artifacts.title: Fig. 1 Flowchart of the Delphi study
artifacts.description: Step 1: In response to the lack of agreement on clinical decisions for children with CM1, the multidisciplinary panel drafted 57 evidence-based statements. Step 2: 35 international experts were invited in Jun-Jul 2019. Step 3: In Sept 2019, 34 experts participated in the first Delphi round; 30/57 statements were endorsed (52.6%). Step 4: In Oct 2019, 27/57 (47%) statements were revised: 15 were rewritten, 11 were reworded, 1 was deleted, and 3 were added. Step 5: In the second round in Oct 2019, 33/34 experts participated (97%) and endorsed 56/59 statements (94.9%). Step 6: At the third round in November 2019, during the Chiari Consensus Conference in Milan, Italy, 33/34 experts participated, including two e-voters; 58/59 statements were endorsed (98.3%). The resulting document contained 58 statements.
artifacts.summary: The flowchart traces how draft statements were revised and voted on across three Delphi rounds. It explains how the pediatric consensus document was produced.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It shows the level of expert agreement behind the statements while distinguishing consensus from a formal grading of evidence.

recommendations.statement: Follow asymptomatic children with incidentally discovered CM1 and no syringomyelia neurologically and with whole-neuraxis MRI until growth ends; individualize the timetable to the clinical findings and extent of tonsillar descent.
recommendations.rationale: A minority of initially asymptomatic children may progress clinically or radiologically.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 2 Planning for CM1 in children: symptoms and followup

recommendations.statement: Ensure neuro-pediatric evaluation for every child with CM1 who has headache.
recommendations.rationale: Differentiating Chiari-related headache from migraine or other headaches is important for an appropriate surgical decision.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 2 Planning for CM1 in children: symptoms and followup

recommendations.statement: Ensure neuro-pediatric evaluation to identify coexisting disorders when a child with CM1 has symptoms or signs of brainstem, cerebellar, or cervical spinal cord dysfunction.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 2 Planning for CM1 in children: symptoms and followup

recommendations.statement: Ensure neuro-pediatric evaluation for children with CM1 and cognitive or behavioral disorders.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 2 Planning for CM1 in children: symptoms and followup

recommendations.statement: Use somatosensory evoked potentials (SEPs) in children with CM1 only alongside other clinical and investigative tools.
recommendations.rationale: Neurophysiological examinations are not routine first-line assessments, and their diagnostic role remains unproven.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 2 Planning for CM1 in children: symptoms and followup

recommendations.statement: Use auditory evoked potentials (BAEPs) in children with CM1 only in conjunction with other clinical and investigative tools.
recommendations.rationale: Neurophysiological examinations are not routine first-line assessments, and their diagnostic role remains unproven.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 2 Planning for CM1 in children: symptoms and followup

recommendations.statement: Use motor evoked potentials (MEPs) in children with CM1 only together with other clinical and investigative tools.
recommendations.rationale: Neurophysiological examinations are not routine first-line assessments, and their diagnostic role remains unproven.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 2 Planning for CM1 in children: symptoms and followup

recommendations.statement: Perform polysomnography in very young children (< 6 years), when apnea is suspected, or when cerebellar tonsillar descent is severe.
recommendations.rationale: Sleep-disordered breathing occurs in children with CM1, and polysomnography can confirm apnea.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 2 Planning for CM1 in children: symptoms and followup

recommendations.statement: In a symptomatic child with CM1 and hydrocephalus, treat the hydrocephalus first to lower raised intracranial pressure and avoid postoperative complications; treat CM1 subsequently if symptoms persist.
recommendations.rationale: Treating hydrocephalus can improve CM1 and syringomyelia without a separate CM1 operation.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 3 Planning for CM1 in children: associated malformations

recommendations.statement: Treat non-syndromic craniosynostosis, including sagittal or lambdoid synostosis and oxycephaly, before addressing CM1 in an affected child.
recommendations.rationale: Craniosynostosis may contribute to acquired CM1.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 3 Planning for CM1 in children: associated malformations

recommendations.statement: For an infant with syndromic craniosynostosis and CM1, first expand cranial volume using vault remodeling appropriate to the syndrome.
recommendations.rationale: Restoring adequate cranial volume is an important part of managing this combination.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 3 Planning for CM1 in children: associated malformations

recommendations.statement: When CM1 persists after cranioplasty in a child with syndromic craniosynostosis, choose the surgical approach according to the syndrome, cranial volume achieved previously, posterior fossa volume, CM1 symptoms, and associated syringomyelia.
recommendations.rationale: Clinical and radiological recurrence is frequent in this population.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 3 Planning for CM1 in children: associated malformations

recommendations.statement: Consider posterior vault osteogenic distraction before posterior fossa decompression in toddlers with CM1, polisynostosis, and predominant brachycephaly, and in selected children of other ages.
recommendations.rationale: Posterior distraction may address both the craniosynostosis and associated CM1 in children with synostotic brachycephaly.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 3 Planning for CM1 in children: associated malformations

recommendations.statement: Before craniovertebral decompression in a child with CM1 and syndromic craniosynostosis, obtain Angio-RM or angio-CT to exclude anomalous subcutaneous drainage.
recommendations.rationale: Identifying anomalous drainage is necessary for surgical planning.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 3 Planning for CM1 in children: associated malformations

recommendations.statement: When tethered cord syndrome coexists with CM1 in a child, perform de-tethering to prevent neuro-urological deterioration, without expecting it to affect CM1.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 3 Planning for CM1 in children: associated malformations

recommendations.statement: Reserve intradural section of the filum terminale in a child with CM1 for treatment of tethered cord syndrome; do not use it to manage a possible CM1 syndrome.
recommendations.rationale: The procedure has no role in treating the associated CM1.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 3 Planning for CM1 in children: associated malformations

recommendations.statement: Do not use extradural section of the filum terminale to treat either tethered cord syndrome or a possible CM1 syndrome in a child with CM1.
recommendations.rationale: The experts identified no evidence supporting either use.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 3 Planning for CM1 in children: associated malformations

recommendations.statement: For a symptomatic child with CM1 but no syringomyelia, bony decompression of the posterior fossa alone may be performed if the family accepts that another operation might become necessary.
recommendations.rationale: Bony decompression alone has a low complication rate but carries a risk of persistent or recurrent symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 4 Surgery for CM1 in children: techniques

recommendations.statement: Prefer bony decompression with duraplasty for a child with CM1 and syringomyelia.
recommendations.context: Delphi agreement: 81.8%. The accompanying discussion cautions that this preference is not an absolute rule for every syrinx.
recommendations.rationale: Duraplasty may provide more consistent improvement but has a higher complication risk than bony decompression alone.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 4 Surgery for CM1 in children: techniques

recommendations.statement: Center bony posterior fossa decompression on an adequate foramen magnum opening, always include C1 laminectomy, and do not extend the decompression to C2 because of the risk of CVJ instability.
recommendations.rationale: The critical region is the bulbocervical junction; unnecessary extension may increase instability risk.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 4 Surgery for CM1 in children: techniques

recommendations.statement: Preserve the arachnoid membrane during CM1 surgery when arachnoiditis is absent.
recommendations.rationale: Arachnoid violation increases the risks of CSF leakage and later scarring.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 4 Surgery for CM1 in children: techniques

recommendations.statement: Use cerebellar tonsillar coagulation or resection when tonsils lie very low and syringomyelia is recurrent or residual.
recommendations.rationale: The maneuver can create space but adds morbidity and a risk of arachnoid scarring.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 4 Surgery for CM1 in children: techniques

recommendations.statement: Prefer autologous or allograft dural patches over artificial grafts; either preferred material is suitable according to the surgeon's preference.
recommendations.rationale: Experiences cited in the consensus suggest avoiding artificial grafts because of graft-related complications.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 4 Surgery for CM1 in children: techniques

recommendations.statement: To help prevent CSF leakage, make the dural closure watertight with non-resorbable stitches and close the muscle and soft tissues securely.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 4 Surgery for CM1 in children: techniques

recommendations.statement: Assess early surgical outcome at 6 and 12 months with clinical examination and whole-neuraxis MRI; cine-MRI may assist.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Surgical outcomes

recommendations.statement: Use persistence of Chiari symptoms 12 months after surgery as the clinical definition of surgical failure.
recommendations.rationale: This interval is usually sufficient for clinical improvement to become apparent, including after bony decompression.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Surgical outcomes

recommendations.statement: When inadequate bony decompression causes failure, evaluate the opening with 3D CT scan and widen the decompression.
recommendations.rationale: An opening that is too small or has undergone bone regrowth can cause failure.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Diagnosis and treatment of the main causes of surgical failure

recommendations.statement: For failure associated with posterior fossa arachnoiditis, use adhesiolysis and/or tonsillar resection; IV ventricle stenting to maintain communication with the perimedullary space is a possible additional procedure.
recommendations.context: Delphi agreement: 87.9%. The role of IV ventricle stenting remains debated.
recommendations.rationale: Postoperative arachnoiditis can cause clinical or radiological recurrence.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Diagnosis and treatment of the main causes of surgical failure

recommendations.statement: When intracranial hypertension is present after CM1 surgery, obtain angio-MRI for venous assessment and 3DCT scan to investigate other causes of raised ICP, including pseudotumor, hydrocephalus, or craniosynostosis.
recommendations.context: Raised ICP is identified as a possible cause of surgical failure.
recommendations.rationale: Recognizing an alternative cause of raised ICP may prevent an unnecessary CM1 reoperation.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Diagnosis and treatment of the main causes of surgical failure

recommendations.statement: Investigate possible CVJ instability with a dynamic CVJ study when assessing surgical failure, particularly in patients with CM 1.5.
recommendations.rationale: Unrecognized CVJ instability can contribute to persistent symptoms after surgery.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Diagnosis and treatment of the main causes of surgical failure

recommendations.statement: Reoperate when postoperative CSF leakage is symptomatic.
recommendations.rationale: The discussion calls for surgical revision of a true leak or symptomatic CSF collection.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Surgical re-intervention

recommendations.statement: Use conservative management first for an asymptomatic postoperative CSF collection.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Surgical re-intervention

recommendations.statement: If a CSF collection persists or increases despite conservative care, reassess the diagnosis before deciding whether to operate.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Surgical re-intervention

recommendations.statement: Observe an asymptomatic child with persistent tonsillar descent but no syrinx for at least 24 months after surgery to detect emerging symptoms.
recommendations.rationale: Persistent radiological tonsillar ectopia alone is not regarded as surgical failure.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Surgical re-intervention

recommendations.statement: Closely follow an asymptomatic child whose syrinx remains visible on MRI at 12 months after surgery; reoperate if scoliosis or symptoms appear.
recommendations.rationale: An unchanged syrinx without symptoms is not, by itself, treated as an automatic indication for reoperation.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Surgical re-intervention

recommendations.statement: Reoperate on a child who remains symptomatic at 6 or 12 months after surgery and whose MRI is unchanged, with no tonsillar ascent and absent flow.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Surgical re-intervention

recommendations.statement: Reoperate on a child with persistent symptoms and syringomyelia on MRI at 6 or 12 months after surgery.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Surgical re-intervention

recommendations.statement: After successful surgery, provide long-term clinical examination and whole-neuraxis MRI for at least 10 years or until growth ends, using a timetable tailored to clinical and MRI findings.
recommendations.rationale: Long-term surveillance is intended to detect recurrence.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 5 Surgery for CM1 in children: outcomes, failure, re-intervention — Surgical re-intervention

recommendations.statement: Operate on CM 1.5 associated with basilar invagination or impressio basilaris only when related symptoms are present.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 6 Specific conditions related to CVJ malformations: surgical options

recommendations.statement: For symptomatic basilar invagination associated with CM1 but without atlanto-axial instability, anterior decompression could be the preferred etiological operation if posterior reduction has failed.
recommendations.rationale: Attempting posterior reduction first can establish whether the odontoid is reducible and may avoid unnecessary anterior decompression.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 6 Specific conditions related to CVJ malformations: surgical options

recommendations.statement: Prefer posterior fixation for basilar invagination accompanied by atlanto-axial dislocation.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 6 Specific conditions related to CVJ malformations: surgical options

recommendations.statement: Include dynamic X-rays and a dynamic CT scan with 3D reconstructions, in addition to MRI, in the standard assessment of CVJ instability in CM.
recommendations.context: Delphi agreement: 81%. The discussion distinguishes this fuller assessment from simple diagnosis, for which it considers dynamic X-rays and MRI sufficient.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 6 Specific conditions related to CVJ malformations: surgical options

recommendations.statement: Do not perform CVJ fixation, whether or not posterior decompression is added, in a patient with CM1 unless CVJ instability has been documented.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 6 Specific conditions related to CVJ malformations: surgical options

recommendations.statement: Prefer posterior decompression together with CVJ fixation for a patient with CM, CVJ instability, and related symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 6 Specific conditions related to CVJ malformations: surgical options

recommendations.statement: Before choosing CVJ instrumentation in a patient with CM, establish the vertebral artery course using preoperative Angio-MRI or Angio-CT and assess occipital crest bone thickness, C2 isthmus diameter, and C3 lateral mass volume.
recommendations.rationale: The relevant anatomy may vary substantially with age.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 6 Specific conditions related to CVJ malformations: surgical options

recommendations.statement: Before selecting C1–C2 instrumentation, establish the vertebral artery course with preoperative angio-MRI or angio-CT and determine the C2 isthmus diameter.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 6 Specific conditions related to CVJ malformations: surgical options

recommendations.statement: Choose between C0-C3 and C1-C2 fixation for a patient with CM and CVJ instability according to local anatomy.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 6 Specific conditions related to CVJ malformations: surgical options

recommendations.statement: In a child with non-Chiari syringomyelia, include whole-neuraxis MRI in the diagnostic assessment to identify an associated dysraphism.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 7 Isolated/non-CM1 syringomyelia in children: differential diagnosis, surgical indications, and techniques

recommendations.statement: In a child with non-Chiari syringomyelia, obtain contrast-enhanced MRI to investigate a spinal cord tumor.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 7 Isolated/non-CM1 syringomyelia in children: differential diagnosis, surgical indications, and techniques

recommendations.statement: In a child with non-Chiari syringomyelia, use dynamic studies to investigate congenital or acquired spinal cord instability.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 7 Isolated/non-CM1 syringomyelia in children: differential diagnosis, surgical indications, and techniques

recommendations.statement: In a child with non-Chiari syringomyelia, use CISS-sequence MRI and/or myelo-CT to investigate associated arachnoidal cysts or arachnoiditis.
recommendations.rationale: These investigations may reveal small cysts or signs of arachnoiditis, although their sensitivity is not absolute.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 7 Isolated/non-CM1 syringomyelia in children: differential diagnosis, surgical indications, and techniques

recommendations.statement: Follow an asymptomatic child with isolated syringomyelia clinically and radiologically rather than operating solely for a stable syrinx.
recommendations.rationale: The reported risk of progression in asymptomatic, isolated, stable syringomyelia is low.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 7 Isolated/non-CM1 syringomyelia in children: differential diagnosis, surgical indications, and techniques

recommendations.statement: Operate when syringomyelia enlarges or becomes symptomatic, including when neurological or neurophysiological deterioration occurs.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 7 Isolated/non-CM1 syringomyelia in children: differential diagnosis, surgical indications, and techniques

recommendations.statement: Surgery for syringomyelia is indicated when a child with isolated syringomyelia develops progressive scoliosis.
recommendations.context: Delphi agreement: 88.2%. The discussion specifies that progression of scoliosis should be associated with a large syrinx to serve as a surgical indication.
recommendations.rationale: Progressive scoliosis can indicate progression of pediatric syringomyelia.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 7 Isolated/non-CM1 syringomyelia in children: differential diagnosis, surgical indications, and techniques

recommendations.statement: Perform de-tethering for syringomyelia associated with spinal dysraphism.
recommendations.rationale: Treatment is directed at the cause of the syringomyelia.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 7 Isolated/non-CM1 syringomyelia in children: differential diagnosis, surgical indications, and techniques

recommendations.statement: Remove an associated spinal cord tumor to treat the syringomyelia.
recommendations.rationale: Treatment is directed at the cause of the syringomyelia.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 7 Isolated/non-CM1 syringomyelia in children: differential diagnosis, surgical indications, and techniques

recommendations.statement: Perform adhesiolysis for symptomatic or progressive syringomyelia caused by arachnoiditis after trauma and/or surgery.
recommendations.context: Delphi agreement: 100%. The discussion cautions that results may be disappointing.
recommendations.rationale: The operation addresses the adhesions associated with the syringomyelia.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 7 Isolated/non-CM1 syringomyelia in children: differential diagnosis, surgical indications, and techniques

recommendations.statement: If symptomatic or progressive syringomyelia persists after prior etiological treatments have failed, a spino-peritoneal, spino-subarachnoidal, or spino-pleural shunt may be performed.
recommendations.context: Delphi agreement: 90.9%. Prior treatments identified in the table are de-tethering, tumor removal, and adhesiolysis.
recommendations.rationale: Direct drainage is reserved for failure of treatment directed at the underlying cause.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 7 Isolated/non-CM1 syringomyelia in children: differential diagnosis, surgical indications, and techniques

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Asymptomatic children with incidentally identified, isolated CM1 and no syringomyelia, including those with tonsillar ectopia ≥ 20 mm.
decision_rules: Do not use the extent of tonsillar descent alone to justify surgery in an asymptomatic child without syringomyelia.
Continue neurological and imaging surveillance until growth is complete; individualize its frequency according to clinical findings and tonsillar herniation.

recommended_regimens.name: Conservative management
recommended_regimens.summary: Observe rather than operate, with neurological follow-up and MRI of the whole neuraxis.

not_recommended.name: Surgery for asymptomatic isolated CM1 without syringomyelia
not_recommended.reason: The consensus does not identify a surgical indication in this population, even when tonsillar ectopia is ≥ 20 mm.

response_assessment.method: Neurological assessment and whole neuraxis MRI at an individualized schedule.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess for emerging symptoms or radiological progression; most asymptomatic children remain stable, although progression is possible.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: If MRI is obtained, it should cover the brain and entire spinal cord. Controls at 1, 3, and 5 years are discussed as examples rather than a fixed schedule.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Asymptomatic children with incidentally discovered CM1 and syringomyelia.
decision_rules: Surgery is indicated when the syrinx is larger than 5–8 mm or a smaller syrinx is enlarging.
The size threshold remains debated; progression of the syrinx is a clearer consideration than its size alone.
The development of symptoms is a principal reason to operate regardless of syrinx size.

recommended_regimens.name: Foramen magnum decompression
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider operative decompression when an asymptomatic child's syrinx meets the stated size or progression criteria; select the operative technique according to the individual presentation.

response_assessment.method: Clinical evaluation and MRI assessment of the syrinx.
response_assessment.interpretation: New symptoms or syrinx enlargement affect the decision to operate.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document cautions against treating the choice of duraplasty for every syrinx as an absolute rule.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with CM1 and epilepsy, without a separate CM1-related indication for surgery.
decision_rules: Do not offer CM1 surgery as a treatment intended to improve seizure control.

not_recommended.name: Surgical treatment of CM1 for seizure control
not_recommended.reason: Surgical treatment of CM1 does not improve the seizure disorder; the document describes the association as incidental.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with CM1 and cognitive and/or behavioral disorders, such as autism, particularly when communication impairment limits symptom reporting.
decision_rules: Carefully assess clinically and instrumentally for manifestations of cerebellar tonsillar ectopia when the child cannot reliably describe symptoms.
Obtain neuro-pediatric evaluation.
Without clear CM1 symptoms, do not operate with the aim of improving cognitive or behavioral findings.

recommended_regimens.name: Careful clinical and instrumental assessment
recommended_regimens.summary: Look for CM1-related signs and symptoms that communication difficulties may obscure before determining whether a separate surgical indication exists.

not_recommended.name: CM1 surgery to improve cognitive and/or behavioral disorders without clear CM1 symptoms
not_recommended.reason: A causal relationship has not been established, and there is no evidence that treating CM1 improves the behavioral disorder.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document notes that cognitive or behavioral improvement after successful surgery in a child who is symptomatic for CM1 can reflect relief of pain or other previously unrecognized symptoms.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with CM1 and headache or symptoms and/or signs suggesting brainstem, cerebellar, or cervical cord dysfunction.
decision_rules: Require neuro-pediatric evaluation before attributing headache or neurological findings to CM1 and deciding on surgery.
Differentiate a possible Chiari headache from migraine and other headache disorders, and identify coexisting conditions.
If CM1-related symptoms are established, their presence is a principal surgical indication regardless of syrinx size.

recommended_regimens.name: Neuro-pediatric evaluation
recommended_regimens.summary: Evaluate symptoms and co-pathologies to support an appropriate decision about CM1 surgery.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Cough- or Valsalva-related, occipital or suboccipital headache lasting a few minutes is discussed as a possible Chiari headache pattern. Polysomnography is indicated in very young children (< 6 years), with suspected apneas, or with severe tonsillar descent. SEPs, BAEPs, and MEPs may supplement, but not replace, other clinical and instrumental assessments.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Symptomatic children with CM1 and hydrocephalus.
decision_rules: Treat hydrocephalus before considering CM1 decompression to relieve raised intracranial pressure and limit postoperative complications.
Consider subsequent CM1 surgery only if symptoms persist after intracranial pressure is adequately controlled.

recommended_regimens.name: Treatment of hydrocephalus
recommended_regimens.summary: Restore CSF pathways and address raised intracranial pressure as the initial intervention.

response_assessment.method: Clinical assessment of symptoms and evaluation of CM1 and any associated syringomyelia.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent symptoms may warrant CM1-directed surgery; improvement may make it unnecessary.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document cites improvement of CM1/syringomyelia after endoscopic third ventriculostomy in many children treated for hydrocephalus, without a subsequent need for specific CM1 or syrinx treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with CM1 and non-syndromic craniosynostosis, including sagittal or lambdoid synostosis and oxycephaly.
decision_rules: Treat the craniosynostosis before addressing CM1.
Consider CM1-directed intervention if symptoms persist after the synostosis has clearly resolved.

recommended_regimens.name: Treatment of craniosynostosis
recommended_regimens.summary: Address the cranial abnormality first, before deciding whether CM1 requires a separate procedure.

response_assessment.method: Assess resolution of the synostosis and persistence of CM1-related symptoms.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent symptoms after clear resolution may justify considering CM1 management.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Infants with CM1 and syndromic craniosynostosis.
decision_rules: Initially increase cranial volume through vault remodeling appropriate to the syndrome.
Assess later CM1 treatment within the broader craniofacial management plan.

recommended_regimens.name: Cranial vault remodeling
recommended_regimens.summary: Perform syndrome-appropriate surgery to expand cranial volume before selecting a CM1-directed operation.

response_assessment.method: Clinical and radiological reassessment of CM1.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent CM1 requires an individualized decision about further intervention.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Specialist craniofacial teams are recommended for this complex presentation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with syndromic craniosynostosis and persistent CM1 after cranioplasty, including toddlers with polisynostosis and predominant brachycephaly.
decision_rules: Base further surgery on the syndrome, cranial volume achieved previously, posterior fossa volume, CM1 symptoms, and associated syringomyelia.
In toddlers with polisynostosis and predominant brachycephaly, and selected children of other ages, consider posterior vault osteogenic distraction before posterior fossa decompression.
If CM1 clearly predominates after intracranial hydrodynamics have been optimized, direct CM1 treatment may be appropriate.
Before craniovertebral decompression, obtain angio-RM or angio-CT to exclude anomalous subcutaneous drainage.

recommended_regimens.name: Individualized craniofacial and CM1 surgical planning
recommended_regimens.summary: Select any repeat intervention according to the syndrome and the results of previous cranial surgery.

alternative_regimens.name: Posterior vault osteogenic distraction
alternative_regimens.summary: May precede posterior fossa decompression in the specified children with synostotic brachycephaly.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Toddlers with polisynostosis and predominant brachycephaly, or selected children in other age groups.

alternative_regimens.name: Posterior fossa decompression
alternative_regimens.summary: May directly address persistent, clinically predominant CM1.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider after adequate optimization of intracranial hydrodynamics and the required vascular assessment.

response_assessment.method: Clinical and radiological assessment of persistent CM1, posterior fossa and cranial volume, and associated syringomyelia.
response_assessment.interpretation: Use the findings and the previous operative result to determine whether and how to reoperate.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Clinical and radiological recurrence is frequent in this population. The document limits the proposed role of posterior osteogenic distraction principally to synostotic brachycephaly.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with CM1 and manifest tethered cord syndrome.
decision_rules: Perform de-tethering to address the tethered cord syndrome and prevent neuro-urological deterioration, not to treat CM1.
For symptomatic tethered cord, the recommended filum terminale approach is intradural section.

recommended_regimens.name: Intradural section of the filum terminale
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat the associated tethered cord syndrome independently of CM1.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The procedure has no influence on CM1.

not_recommended.name: Extradural section of the filum terminale
not_recommended.reason: It is not recommended for either tethered cord syndrome or a possible CM1 syndrome.

not_recommended.name: Intradural section of the filum terminale to treat CM1
not_recommended.reason: Its recommended role is limited to tethered cord syndrome; it does not manage the associated CM1.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The child and family should be told that de-tethering does not address CM1. The proposed association with “occult tethered spinal cord” has never been demonstrated.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Symptomatic children without syringomyelia, particularly without severe symptoms, whose family accepts the possibility of another operation.
decision_rules: Bony posterior fossa decompression alone may be used because its complication rate is low, while acknowledging the possibility of persistent or recurrent symptoms and further surgery.
Center the opening on the foramen magnum and include C1 laminectomy; avoid extension to C2 because of craniovertebral junction instability risk.
Avoid an unnecessarily extensive occipital opening.

recommended_regimens.name: Bony decompression of the posterior fossa alone
recommended_regimens.summary: A possible initial operation for symptomatic CM1 without syringomyelia when the family accepts its potential need for later revision.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The document describes a very low complication rate but a lower success rate than decompression with duraplasty; it provides no numerical efficacy estimate for this comparison.

not_recommended.name: Routine extension of bony decompression to C2
not_recommended.reason: The consensus advises against it because of the risk of CVJ instability.

response_assessment.method: Clinical evaluation and whole neuraxis MRI; cine-MRI may help.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent symptoms and radiological findings guide consideration of revision.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The dimensions of the bone opening should be adapted to the child. The document describes differing panelist preferences concerning initial bony decompression versus duraplasty.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with CM1 and syringomyelia, particularly when symptoms or the syrinx are substantial.
decision_rules: Bony decompression with duraplasty is preferred when syringomyelia is present, but this is not an absolute rule for every syrinx.
Preserve the arachnoid membrane if arachnoiditis is absent.
Limit tonsillar coagulation or resection to very low-lying tonsils and recurrent or residual syringomyelia.
Favor autologous or allograft dural patches over artificial grafts and achieve a watertight closure.

recommended_regimens.name: Bony decompression + duraplasty
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred decompression approach for children with CM1 and syringomyelia, with arachnoid preservation when appropriate and careful dural and soft-tissue closure.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The document describes more consistent radiological results than bony decompression alone, alongside a higher rate of CSF-related complications, without giving numerical efficacy estimates.

alternative_regimens.name: Bony decompression alone
alternative_regimens.summary: May adequately treat a small or asymptomatic syrinx.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when the syrinx is small or asymptomatic rather than assuming that every case of syringomyelia requires duraplasty.

not_recommended.name: Routine opening of the arachnoid membrane without arachnoiditis
not_recommended.reason: Preservation is indicated to reduce CSF leakage and delayed arachnoid scarring.

response_assessment.method: Clinical examination and whole neuraxis MRI; cine-MRI may be useful.
response_assessment.interpretation: Evaluate symptoms, syrinx evolution, tonsillar position, and CSF flow in the clinical context.
