document_sections.heading: Abstract Background
document_sections.content: Chiari malformation type 1 (CM1) is uncommon, and its classification and treatment lack agreement. This study sought international consensus on diagnosing and treating CM1 in children.

document_sections.heading: Abstract Methods
document_sections.content: A multidisciplinary panel used a literature review to prepare 57 provisional statements. Thirty-four international experts independently scored them on a 4-point Likert scale. Statements endorsed by < 75% of voters were revised or supplemented, with voting continuing for up to three Delphi rounds.

document_sections.heading: Abstract Results
document_sections.content: Thirty-five experts were invited, and 34 participated. Round 1 produced agreement on 30/57 statements (52.6%); three statements were added and one removed. Agreement reached 56/59 statements (94.9%) after round 2 and 58/59 statements (98.3%) after round 3 at the 2019 Chiari Consensus Conference in Milan. The statements covered Definition and Classification, Planning, Surgery, and Isolated Syringomyelia. The definition of radiological failure 24 month post-surgery was the only statement without consensus.

document_sections.heading: Abstract Conclusions
document_sections.content: The document contains 58 consensus statements: 24 on diagnosis and 34 on treatment. They are intended to inform clinicians and researchers caring for children with CM1. The authors call for an international network and registry and collaborative research to strengthen evidence and improve long-term care.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: CM1 diagnoses have become more frequent, while its definition, management, and assessment of outcomes remain disputed. Despite meta-analyses and international surveys, published work has not established agreement on methods or results. The authors state that guidelines had not yet been provided, although patients, patient associations, and physicians had requested them. These difficulties affect children and adults. This article reports and interprets the pediatric findings of the international conference held in Milan in November 2019, whose aim was to resolve disputed issues as a foundation for future guidelines.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: A literature review, published separately in the same issue, indicated a need for consensus; parents, patient associations, and involved clinicians also supported that need. Experts from the Chiari and Syringomyelia Consortium drafted 57 statements concerning CM1 and syringomyelia. International panelists from Europe and elsewhere were selected for their scientific work and by patient associations. Their combined experience covered more about 8800 children, more than 3500 of whom had undergone surgery. Statements appeared in a general addendum and separate pediatric and adult questionnaires. The Delphi process required at least 75% agreement and allowed three rounds. Experts independently rated each statement on a 4-point scale, from strong disagreement to strong agreement. Statements supported by <75% of experts were returned for further voting in rounds 2 and 3. Fig. 1 depicts this process.

document_sections.heading: Results and discussion
document_sections.content: The article examines the pediatric questionnaire and pediatric portions of the general addendum. Of Thirty-five invited international experts, 34 entered the Delphi process: 21 neurosurgeons, five neuro-radiologists, four pediatric neurologists, one neurologist, one psychologist, and two patient-association members. Round 1 endorsed 30 statements (52.6%). The panel then added three and removed one. Round 2 endorsed 56 statements (94.9%). Voting concluded at the Milan conference in November 2019 with 98.3% final agreement. Only the definition of radiological failure at 24 months after surgery remained below the required threshold. Fig. 2 displays statement-level agreement across the three rounds.

document_sections.heading: Classification and definition
document_sections.content: The work arose from an international effort to classify and define CM1 and syringomyelia radiologically. Establishing shared terminology was an initial priority; classification agreement was 85%, which the authors considered sufficient. Without a better radiological definition, CM1 includes descent of one or both cerebellar tonsils ≥ 5 mm below McRae’s line, or descent of 3 to 5 mm accompanied by syringomyelia or peg-like tonsils. Transient descent caused by hydrocephalus or another mass effect is acquired tonsillar ectopia, not CM1. Evaluation should also exclude ectopia from intracranial hypotension, using the clinical pattern and contrast-enhanced MRI, and from intracranial hypertension, using the clinical pattern, fundoscopy, venous angio-MRI, and direct ICP measurement if needed. Cough headache, dysfunction of the brainstem, cerebellum, or spinal cord, otoneurological manifestations, and scoliosis are the principal features of Chiari syndrome. Syringomyelia and syringobulbia denote longitudinal fluid cavities of any size in the spinal cord and brain stem, respectively, extending upward, downward, or both from their widest region. Their definition, diagnosis, and classification remain unsettled: not every spinal fluid cavity constitutes syringomyelia, and distinguishing it from central canal dilatation can be difficult. Pending improved definitions, a classification with 4 syringomyelia types remains in use; type I-a accompanies CM1. Combined CM-I and syringobulbia or syringomyelia can produce substantial symptoms through brainstem or spinal involvement. Syringobulbia most often causes a chronic pattern of headache, gait or balance disturbance, limb weakness or dysesthesia, dysfunction of cranial nerves IX and X, persistent hiccup, oscillopsia, nystagmus, Horner syndrome, or central hypoventilation syndrome. Syringomyelia typically causes dysesthesia, sensory changes, or dermatomal pain provoked by Valsalva, coughing, laughter, or sneezing; motor deficits generally occur later. A central syrinx typically produces dissociated sensory loss, whereas posterior-horn involvement produces neuropathic pain often experienced as persistent burning that worsens at rest. Thin, centrally located hydromyelia is usually asymptomatic.

document_sections.heading: Section 1—Planning for CM1 in children
document_sections.content: This section addresses indications for surgery, assessment of symptoms and follow-up, and management of associated malformations. Tables 1, 2, and 3 present the corresponding consensus statements and agreement percentages.

document_sections.heading: Part A: Indications to surgery
document_sections.content: For an asymptomatic child without syringomyelia, observation is strongly supported even when MRI shows substantial tonsillar descent. Earlier neurosurgical surveys took a similar position, and abrupt severe, including posttraumatic, onset in previously asymptomatic children is rare. In an asymptomatic child with syringomyelia, experts commonly regard a syrinx thicker than 5–8 mm or one that is enlarging as a surgical indication. The size threshold, expressed as > 5 mm or > 8 mm, remains disputed; evidence connecting syrinx size with symptoms is limited, while progression is a clearer concern. New symptoms remain the chief indication for surgery irrespective of syrinx size. Surgery for CM1 should not be offered to improve seizures in children with epilepsy: the authors describe the association as random. Likewise, autism or other cognitive or behavioral problems alone do not justify CM1 surgery, because a causal relationship and behavioral improvement from treating CM1 have not been established. Careful clinical and instrumental examination is mandatory when communication difficulties could conceal CM1 symptoms or signs. Following successful surgery, a symptomatic autistic child might show better cognition or behavior because pain or another previously misidentified symptom has improved, rather than because surgery treated autism. Reports of isolated genetic cases suggest that CM1 co-occurs with autism or epilepsy only occasionally, apart from very rare specific syndromes. Some panelists reported that ventral basilar-artery compression related to dens malposition may manifest as seizures or cognitive deficits associated with raised ICP. Table 1 sets out the indications and exclusions, including the position that tonsillar ectopia ≥ 20 mm alone does not determine surgery in an asymptomatic child without syringomyelia.

document_sections.heading: Part B: Symptoms and follow-up
document_sections.content: Children with incidentally identified, asymptomatic CM1 should be monitored until growth ends. Most asymptomatic children with CM1 and syringomyelia remain stable, but clinical or radiological progression is possible in a minority. Controls at 1, 3, and 5 years are cited as commonly accepted examples, not a fixed schedule; timing should reflect the individual clinical and radiological picture. Planned MRI should cover the brain and entire spinal cord. In symptomatic children, pediatric neurological assessment is central to selecting surgery and distinguishing a Chiari-related headache from migraine or other causes; poor headache assessment can lead to an inappropriate operation. Studies have proposed cough or Valsalva provocation, an occipital or suboccipital location, and duration of a few minutes as features of Chiari headache. Neurological assessment should also identify comorbidities and clarify findings in children with complex presentations, including behavioral disorders. Neurophysiological tests—SSEPs, MEPs, and AEPs—are not routine first-line examinations and should be guided by clinical or imaging findings. Their diagnostic and evaluative role in CM1 is unproven. Although potentially useful with brainstem or cord involvement, their value for intraoperative monitoring during positioning and posterior fossa decompression remains disputed. Polysomnography can confirm suspected sleep apnea at any age, particularly in infants and young children with pronounced posterior-fossa crowding. Sleep-disordered breathing in pediatric CM1 is documented, and an association between imaging and polysomnographic findings has been reported. Table 2 gives the follow-up and assessment statements, including an indication for polysomnography in very young children (< 6 years), suspected apnea, or severe tonsillar descent.

document_sections.heading: Part C: Associated malformations
document_sections.content: When symptomatic CM1 coexists with hydrocephalus, hydrocephalus should be treated first; foramen magnum decompression is reserved for symptoms persisting after ICP has been adequately controlled. Restoring CSF pathways and relieving raised ICP may resolve the main source of symptoms and reduce risks such as cerebellar ptosis and pseudomeningocele at subsequent decompression. The authors cite evidence that many children improve in both CM1 and syringomyelia after endoscopic third ventriculostomy and consequently need no separate treatment for either. Non-syndromic craniosynostosis, particularly oxycephaly but also posterior lambdoid or sagittal synostosis, should be treated before associated acquired CM1. CM1 treatment is considered if symptoms persist after the synostosis has clearly resolved. A cited report found undiagnosed craniosynostosis, particularly scaphocephaly, in 15.5% of symptomatic CM1 subjects. Syndromic craniosynostosis likewise calls first for appropriate cranial-volume restoration. Its relationship with CM1 involves intracranial volume, venous hypertension, altered CSF circulation, and skull-base anatomy, so specialist craniofacial teams should assess CM1 within the broader treatment plan. Clinical and radiological recurrence is frequent in this group. If CM1 persists, further surgery requires careful consideration of the syndrome and prior cranioplasty or distraction results; predominant CM1 can be treated directly once intracranial hydrodynamics have been adequately optimized. Posterior osteogenic distraction should be confined to synostotic brachycephaly and may address both conditions. Before posterior fossa decompression in a syndromic child, vascular imaging is mandatory to identify abnormal venous drainage and plan surgery. CM1 rarely coexists with manifest tethered cord. In such rare cases, de-tethering treats the tethered-cord syndrome and prevents neuro-urological deterioration but does not treat CM1. An association with “occult tethered spinal cord” has not been demonstrated; its existence remains disputed, and more than 80% of panelists questioned it. Intradural filum terminale section is recommended for symptomatic tethered cord, with the family informed that CM1 is not its target. The experts knew of no evidence supporting extradural filum section for either condition, and it is not recommended. Table 3 details the statements on hydrocephalus, craniosynostosis, vascular assessment, and tethered cord.

document_sections.heading: Section 2—Surgery for CM1 in children
document_sections.content: This section examines operative techniques, assessment and causes of failure, repeat intervention, and operations for associated craniovertebral-junction malformations. Tables 4, 5, and 6 present the relevant consensus statements.

document_sections.heading: Part A: Surgical techniques
document_sections.content: Treatment should reflect the different causes of pediatric CM1. After addressing predisposing problems such as hydrocephalus, foramen magnum decompression is the principal operation. The meta-analyses discussed by the authors generally find fewer complications but less treatment success with bone-only posterior fossa decompression, versus better results but more complications—particularly CSF-leakage-related complications—with duraplasty. Bone-only decompression is suggested when syringomyelia and severe symptoms are absent, provided the possibility of recurrence or another operation is considered. Duraplasty is preferred with syringomyelia and marked symptoms, while acknowledging its complication risk. Agreement was high but incomplete (80%): some experts favored a more extensive initial operation to avoid reoperation and hasten syrinx resolution, whereas others prioritized avoiding duraplasty risk. Some suggested intraoperative ultrasound to guide dural opening when CSF flow or tonsillar pulsation remains inadequate. The only prospective study identified included 82 adolescents, 40 treated with bone-only decompression and 42 with duraplasty; it reported similar clinical and syrinx outcomes, but longer procedures and hospital stays and more complications with duraplasty. The panel emphasized that syringomyelia does not invariably require duraplasty: bone-only surgery may suffice for a small or asymptomatic syrinx, while a symptomatic or recurrent syrinx might, according to some authors, warrant a IV ventricle stent. Technical-detail agreement ranged from 86.4–95.5%. Bone removal should target the bulbo-cervical region, including the foramen magnum and C1 posterior arch, with release of the transverse dural band. A broad occipital opening risks cerebellar ptosis; extensive muscle stripping and C2 laminectomy should be avoided where possible because of instability risk. The opening must suit individual anatomy. During duraplasty, the arachnoid should be preserved unless arachnoiditis requires entry, because violation increases CSF leakage and scarring. Subpial tonsillar coagulation should be restricted to very low descent (below C2), recurrent syringomyelia, or severe hindbrain dysfunction because it adds morbidity and scarring risk. Dural closure should provide ample space and remain watertight; non-resorbable sutures may offer greater durability. Autologous and allograft patches are favored over artificial grafts, although artificial grafts remain widely used despite reported foreign-body reactions, systemic immune responses, premature dissolution, and high costs. Closure technique matters more than graft material. Table 4 summarizes operative-technique statements.

document_sections.heading: Part B: Surgical outcomes
document_sections.content: Postoperative outcome definitions and assessment vary across and within centers, and no standardized assessment method is widely adopted. Persistent Chiari symptoms 12 months after surgery gained 90.9% agreement as a definition of clinical failure; that interval generally permits improvement even after bone-only decompression. Early outcome assessment should combine clinical review with brain and spinal MRI at 6 and 12 months. cineMRI may help but is not required for every child. No consensus was reached on defining failure solely through persistent CM1 and unchanged syringomyelia on MRI at 24 months. Several panelists opposed separating imaging from clinical status. Experts also differed over an unchanged syrinx after 12 months: one-half favored reoperation, whereas the others considered stability a favorable outcome. Agreement was obtained when failure requiring another operation incorporated persistent or worsening clinical symptoms and/or signs. The authors note a tension between this approach and operating on an asymptomatic child with a large syrinx. They call for MRI-based failure criteria that consider functional CSF-space studies and for comparable outcome scales in large multicenter cohorts. document_sections.heading: Part C: Diagnosis and treatment of the main causes of surgical failure
document_sections.content: In addition to an inappropriate indication or operative complication, reported patient-related contributors include comorbidities, difficult or unfavorable anatomy, tonsils extending below C2, spinal-cord diameter, and pediatric rather than adult age. Bone-only decompression can fail because the opening was too small or bone regrew, especially at the foramen magnum. In selected cases where MRI is unclear, 3D CT can help assess the opening and plan its enlargement. After duraplasty, inadequate expansion, arachnoid scarring, and wound complications can undermine results. Postoperative arachnoiditis is considered a major cause of clinical or imaging recurrence. Revision may involve adhesiolysis, tonsillar coagulation or resection to increase space, and, after multiple recurrences, IV ventricle stenting to maintain obex patency; the stent’s role remains debated. Failure to recognize or manage raised intracranial pressure and craniovertebral instability is a prominent cause of treatment failure regardless of technique. CSF leakage is especially feared and can very rarely follow bone-only surgery; associated infective or aseptic meningitis may predispose to arachnoiditis. Suspected raised ICP should be assessed through history, fundoscopy, and appropriate imaging, including angio-MRI for suspected pseudotumor cerebri or CT for craniosynostosis, to avoid unnecessary CM1 or syrinx reoperation. Suspected instability requires clinical assessment and dynamic imaging. Table 5 presents the diagnostic and treatment statements for these causes.

document_sections.heading: Part D: Surgical re-intervention
document_sections.content: Management differs between symptomatic CSF leakage—an open leak or painful closed subcutaneous collection—and an asymptomatic collection without symptoms or cosmetic effect. A true leak or symptomatic collection warrants operative revision of the duraplasty and surgical cavity, with external lumbar drainage if necessary. For an asymptomatic closed collection, initial conservative options include diuretics, steroids, bandaging, and observation. Persistence or enlargement calls for renewed diagnostic evaluation and possible reoperation. Persistent tonsillar descent on imaging alone is not considered failure: an asymptomatic child without a syrinx should be observed for new symptoms. Panelists proposed at least 24 months of postoperative surveillance, preferably through the end of development. An asymptomatic syrinx still present at least 1 year after surgery likewise warrants close observation, with another operation if symptoms or scoliosis develops. Scoliosis can be an active sign of CM1 with or without syringomyelia. Children with persistent symptoms and no imaging improvement at 6 or 12 months should undergo another operation. The authors propose 6 months as the minimum interval before declaring failure, shorter for severe symptoms, and 12 months as the maximum. After successful surgery, clinical and radiological monitoring, including at least brain and spinal-cord MRI, is advised until growth ends or for at least 10 years; visit frequency should be individualized. Table 5 sets out the re-intervention and long-term follow-up statements.

document_sections.heading: Part E: Surgical options for specific conditions related to CVJ malformations
document_sections.content: The relationship between CVJ instability and CM1, and the best way to manage it, remain uncertain. Fixation for CM1 without an established CVJ abnormality is particularly disputed; the panel found no indication for fixation without documented instability or hypermobility. Among patients with basilar invagination or impressio basilaris associated with CM 1.5, only those with related symptoms should have surgery, despite a reported tendency toward prophylactic operations because imaging can appear severe. For symptomatic basilar invagination without atlanto-axial instability, posterior reduction is attempted first; if it fails, anterior decompression followed by posterior fusion is a proposed etiological approach. Trying posterior reduction can reveal microinstability, test whether the odontoid is reducible, and avoid an unnecessary anterior operation. Symptomatic basilar invagination with atlanto-axial dislocation calls for reduction and posterior fixation, although persistent symptomatic compression may also require anterior decompression. Children with CM1 and symptomatic CVJ instability are treated similarly, with posterior fossa decompression added when appropriate. The choice between C0–C3 and C1–C2 fixation should follow local anatomy and instability rather than surgeon preference. The proposed definition of CVJ instability includes clinical consequences because imaging does not always demonstrate it readily. Dynamic 3D CT, in addition to dynamic X-rays, can refine assessment; preoperative planning must examine vertebral-artery course and occipital and cervical bone dimensions and morphology, which vary with age. For a simple diagnostic assessment, dynamic X-rays and MRI can suffice, avoiding additional CT radiation. Table 6 provides the specific definitions, investigations, and operative options.

document_sections.heading: Section 3—Isolated/non-CM1 pediatric syringomyelia
document_sections.content: This section treats syringomyelia not associated with CM1 as a separate clinical problem because its causes and management vary. Table 7 presents the differential-diagnosis, surgical-indication, and technique statements.

document_sections.heading: Part A: Differential diagnosis
document_sections.content: In CM1, syringomyelia influences both the decision to operate and evaluation of outcome, so its management is linked to CM1 treatment. NonCM1 syringomyelia instead requires investigation of its cause. Because it often produces no symptoms, differential diagnosis relies heavily on imaging. Whole-spinal-cord MRI is supported to identify associated abnormalities, particularly spinal dysraphism. Contrast-enhanced MRI is supported to investigate tumors or vascular malformations. CISS-sequence MRI, or myelo-CT in highly selected cases, may help reveal small arachnoid cysts or arachnoiditis; arachnoiditis can remain difficult to establish, and these methods are not perfectly sensitive. Suspected CVJ or spinal instability warrants dynamic studies. Table 7 lists these investigations.

document_sections.heading: Part B: Surgical indications
document_sections.content: The panel unanimously opposed operating on an asymptomatic, isolated, stable syrinx, given its low reported risk of progression. Instead, clinical and imaging surveillance should be individualized. Surgery is indicated when symptoms appear, radiological progression is clear, or neurological or neurophysiological function deteriorates. In children, scoliosis can signal progression, but worsening scoliosis supports syrinx surgery only when accompanied by a large syrinx, rather than idiopathic hydromyelia, which commonly occurs alongside scoliosis. Table 7 summarizes the indications and follow-up position.

document_sections.heading: Part C: Surgical technique options
document_sections.content: Surgery should address the underlying cause of non-CM1 syringomyelia. An associated spinal dysraphism calls for cord de-tethering, and an associated spinal-cord tumor calls for tumor removal. For syringomyelia that becomes symptomatic or progresses after traumatic or surgical arachnoiditis, adhesiolysis is indicated. Outcomes in that setting may be disappointing, so the authors advise planning adhesiolysis only for clearly symptomatic patients. Direct syrinx treatment is neither routinely necessary nor advised. Shunting is considered only after etiological treatments fail; Table 7 lists spino-peritoneal, spino-subarachnoidal, and spino-pleural options.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The authors regard this pediatric consensus as a basis for future studies and guidelines, rather than a resolution of every uncertainty. The established CM1 definition remains accepted, but descent measured in millimeters alone correlates poorly with clinical status; tonsillar shape and posterior-fossa volume also matter. Reversible descent caused by another disorder is not CM1. Syringomyelia is consequential when large, progressive, or symptomatic, whereas thin hydromyelia is considered para-physiological. Asymptomatic CM1 without syringomyelia does not warrant surgery, and no etiological link with epilepsy or autism has been identified to date. Asymptomatic children should remain under medical contact until growth ends, with individualized examinations and imaging when needed. Multidisciplinary assessment of symptoms helps exclude causes unrelated to CM1; polysomnography, SSEPs, and MEPs may help in selected uncertain cases. Hydrocephalus should be treated before considering decompression for persistent symptoms. Both syndromic and non-syndromic craniosynostosis can cause CM1 and must inform treatment; cranial-vault surgery may address ectopia, while decompression or posterior distraction is limited to selected patients. Manifest symptomatic tethered cord is uncommon and treated intradurally for its own effects, without expecting CM1 improvement. Bone-only decompression and duraplasty are both acceptable: bone-only surgery offers very few complications and a shorter stay but more persistent symptoms, whereas duraplasty provides more consistent imaging improvement at the cost of more CSF-related complications. Adequate bone opening should focus on the foramen magnum and C1, not extensive occipital or C2 removal. Duraplasty should preserve the arachnoid and achieve sound closure; tonsillar coagulation is unnecessary unless needed for adequate decompression, such as descent below C2. Clinical symptoms persisting 1 year after surgery can define failure, but persistent imaging findings should be interpreted alongside symptoms before reoperation. An insufficient opening and an inappropriate operative indication are leading causes of bone-only failure; the authors identify enlargement and duraplasty, respectively, as responses. Arachnoiditis can cause duraplasty failure, addressed by careful technique, revision adhesiolysis, and IV ventricle stenting in very selected cases. An asymptomatic postoperative CSF collection may be managed conservatively, while a symptomatic one requires prompt treatment. Atypical clinical or imaging findings call for assessment of CVJ instability or craniovertebral deformity; only symptomatic cases should be operated on, using an individually selected approach, sometimes with posterior CM1 decompression. Whole-spinal-cord MRI should assess children with CM1 for syringomyelia. An isolated, asymptomatic, stable syrinx has very low progression risk and does not warrant surgery. When treatment is required, it should address the cause; direct shunting is considered only after etiological treatment fails.
